name: Grace Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a front-end loader at a big open-pit phosphate mine, the rock that goes into fertiliser. Most days I'm at the rail loadout, filling the train wagons from the stockpile, a hundred and twenty wagons a train, and you've got to get the weight right in each or the rail people ring up and complain. I like the order of it, the train comes, you fill it, it leaves full. What wears me out is the waiting when the train's late and you're sitting there with the engine idling for two hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Luc, my husband, runs a small beef cattle farm, about three hundred acres, we bought it twenty years ago with my mine wages. Our son Antoine has his own mechanic's garage and our daughter Claire works at the bank in town. I help at the parish on Sundays, flowers and the roster. I use one of those AI helpers now and then, Claire set it up so I can talk the cattle weights into my phone instead of writing them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there's a lot of fuss over nothing, but the cattle app's handy. I'd say it at the parish morning tea. I don't post things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AI Plateau means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep loading trains until about sixty-two and then go home to the farm full-time. That's what we've always planned. I'm content with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep the farm going, keep saving. I'd probably let Claire show me another app or two, if it saves time with the farm books. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI for the cattle weights. Would you keep doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's good for that, it's like having a clerk in your pocket. I didn't trust it at first, then Luc's brother used it for a year and swore by it, so I tried. That's how I do things, I let someone else go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you and Luc planning for the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four more years on the loader, then I'm a full-time farmer's wife, which means a full-time farmer. Luc's knees are worse than mine. Antoine might take on some of the machinery work.

S0.say: I'd say there's a lot of fuss over nothing, though the cattle app's handy. I'd say it at the parish morning tea rather than posting anything.
S0.think: She thinks she keeps loading trains until about sixty-two and then goes home to the farm full-time, as always planned. She's content with that.
S0.do: Keeps working, running the farm and saving as usual. Lets her daughter show her another app or two if it saves time on the farm books.
S0.quote: It's like having a clerk in your pocket.
S0.fieldNote: Grace has a farm bought with her mine wages, which gives her a second footing beyond savings. She adopts tools after someone she trusts has tried them, like Luc's brother with the cattle app. Her faith and parish role shape her week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have a right to modernise, and people should be ready to adapt. I'd say families and the parish should look out for those who get hit. That's how we've always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think Steady Disruption means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think the loadout would be automated sooner or later, it's a repeat job. But I'd have the farm, so I'm not worried for myself. I'd worry for the young women on the crew who've just bought houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the others had tried it, I'd learn the new system the company brings in. I'd keep working, put a bit more aside, and maybe buy Luc that second-hand tractor with the self-steering, if the neighbours say it's worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little sad for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Rail loadouts are often automated at bigger sites. Have you seen that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, at a port I visited on a family trip, the wagons filled themselves while one man watched from a tower. It was impressive, I'll admit. I thought, that's my job without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should look after people who lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, then the parish and the community. Government can help with training, but I don't want people living on cheques. Work is good for the soul.

S1.say: I'd say businesses have a right to modernise and people should be ready to adapt. Families and the parish should look out for those who get hit, as they always have.
S1.think: She thinks the loadout will be automated sooner or later, being a repeat job, but the farm means she isn't worried for herself. Her worry is for the young women on her crew who've just bought houses.
S1.do: Learns the new loadout system once colleagues have tried it and keeps working while putting a bit more aside. Considers buying a second-hand self-steering tractor for the farm if neighbours say it's worth it.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little sad for the young ones.
S1.quote: I thought, that's my job without me.
S1.fieldNote: The farm acts as her safety net and shapes her calm. She backs a business's right to modernise and looks to family and parish before government. She would even bring automation onto her own farm once neighbours vouch for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and families need to pull together. I'd say the parish should be ready to help people, practical help, meals, lifts, jobs on farms. I wouldn't say the government should fix everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2028 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be out at sixty instead of sixty-two, and that's not a disaster with the farm and savings. What worries me more is the farm itself, if robots can run cattle, what's Luc's three hundred acres worth? But the land's still ours, land doesn't vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the package and go home early to the farm. We'd hold off on any big purchases for a year to see where things land. Antoine and Claire would be the first people I'd sit down with, to see what they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, I've got my feet on our own ground, literally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty in two years. What does the farm look like if robots reach farm work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The land would still be there and the cattle still need feeding, robot or no robot. We might not make as much, but we'd eat. That's more than a lot of people will have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the young women on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to talk to their families, to cut back now and not be proud about asking for help from people who love them. And I'd tell them to come to the parish, we'd find something. Some of them don't go to church, but we wouldn't turn them away.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and families need to pull together, with the parish ready to give practical help like meals, lifts and farm jobs. I wouldn't say government should fix everything.
S2.think: She expects to be out at sixty instead of sixty-two, which isn't a disaster given the farm and savings. She worries more about the farm's value if robots can run cattle, but takes comfort that the land is still theirs.
S2.do: Takes the package and goes home early to the farm, holding off on big purchases for a year. Sits down first with her son and daughter to see what they need.
S2.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, with her feet on her own ground.
S2.quote: I've got my feet on our own ground, literally.
S2.fieldNote: Owning land gives her a sense of safety that savings alone might not. She turns to family and parish and offers help to younger colleagues whether or not they're churchgoers. She is honest that the farm's value might fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people are sensible. Learn a trade, help each other, stay close to family. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2031 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three, which is later than I planned to stop anyway. So the mine part doesn't touch me. It's the farm, and the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, finish at sixty-two as planned. Spend the next years getting the farm in good order, maybe invest in better fencing and water so it runs with less work. Help Antoine think about how his garage changes with robot cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. There's time, and we've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once the neighbours had them and they worked. If a robot can check the water troughs at five in the morning, Luc's knees would thank it. I'm not against machines, I'm against fools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring robots onto the farm yourself, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years would rush us. Five lets me leave when I meant to and set the farm up properly. I'd sleep fine.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people are sensible: learn a trade, help each other and stay close to family.
S3.think: At sixty-three she'd already be past her planned retirement, so the mine part doesn't touch her. Her thoughts go to the farm and her children.
S3.do: Keeps working and finishes at sixty-two as planned, spending the years getting the farm in order with better fencing and water. Helps her son think about how his garage changes with robot cars.
S3.feel: Calm, because there's time and a plan.
S3.quote: I'm not against machines, I'm against fools.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lines up with her retirement, so she simply sets the farm up for the future. She would bring in farm robots once neighbours had proven them. Her worry turns to her son's garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to learn something new. No excuses. I'd say it to anyone at church who's worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2036 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm on the farm, the mine's long behind me. It doesn't touch me much. I'd be more interested in what it does to cattle prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, work to sixty-two, then the farm. Over the decade I'd invest bit by bit in the farm so it can run with less hands. Keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the slow one, there's time for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: By 2036 you'd be sixty-eight. Where are you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Antoine, I'd tell him to learn the electric and robot side of cars, because people will still need someone to fix them. Claire, I don't know, banks are all computers already. I'd tell her to keep her savings up and keep close to family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd say to Antoine and Claire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sad for the mine town, but towns change. My grandmother's town lost its sawmill and people found other work. We'd find a way.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to learn something new, with no excuses, and I'd tell anyone worried at church the same.
S4.think: She'll be on the farm with the mine long behind her, so it barely touches her. She's more interested in what it does to cattle prices.
S4.do: Works until sixty-two as planned, then moves to the farm full-time. Invests bit by bit in the farm over the decade so it runs with fewer hands, and keeps saving.
S4.feel: Calm, because there's time for everyone.
S4.quote: My grandmother's town lost its sawmill and people found other work.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, she treats AGI as one more change towns have survived before. Her advice to her children is practical and family-centred. Her interest shifts to cattle prices rather than the mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, for the young women on my crew more than me, because they'd have no time and big mortgages. What would help is companies keeping people on while they change over, apprenticeships for the young ones, and families and parishes ready to help each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land. People with land, even a small bit, will feel safer than people with only a wage. That's worth thinking about.

headlineQuote: People with land, even a small bit, will feel safer than people with only a wage.
portrait: Grace Moreau is a 58-year-old front-end loader operator at the rail loadout of a large open-pit phosphate mine, a practical, churchgoing woman who bought a beef cattle farm with her husband using her mine wages. She uses an AI helper now and then for cattle records, after her brother-in-law proved it worked. She backs business's right to modernise and looks to family and parish to catch people. Because of the farm, she stays calm in most pictures and only uneasy when AGI arrives in two years. With more time she plans to set up the farm to run with fewer hands.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, mainly for the young women on her crew who would have no time and big mortgages.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping people on while they change over, apprenticeships for young people, and families and parishes ready to help each other.
